title: Using Learning Analytics to Study Novice Learners' Work on Quantum Circuit Simulator Tasks
authors: Juuso Jaakola, Vlad Stirbu, Teiko Heinosaari
abstract: Interactive quantum circuit simulators are increasingly used to support introductory quantum computing education for learners from varied disciplinary backgrounds. These environments can also generate detailed response logs of submitted circuits, but such data are rarely transformed into evidence that instructors can use for course redesign and development.   We present a learning analytics framework for quantum circuit simulator tasks and report its task-level branch on anonymised logs from an introductory quantum computing course delivered in the TIM learning environment. The task branch characterises exercises through participation, completion, first-attempt accuracy, valid-attempt counts, sessionised active time, and observed answer-space reporting of common correct and incorrect constructions.   The dataset covers the 2024-2025 cohort of 492 learners, 47,533 valid submissions, and 21 obligatory quantum circuit exercises. The framework identifies bottleneck tasks, broad solution spaces, and recurring wrong-answer patterns that are not visible from final scores alone. Its most distinctive output is a plain-text representation of the observed answer space, designed to make open-ended circuit submissions directly interpretable to instructors. We show how response logs can reveal actionable task-design issues and support concrete course redesign. A learner-level branch is retained only as an ongoing research extension and is not a central empirical contribution of the present paper.
summary: This paper introduces a learning analytics framework to analyze detailed response logs from quantum circuit simulator tasks in an introductory course. By profiling task difficulty and mapping the observed answer space, the authors provide actionable evidence for course designers. This work demonstrates how process data, beyond simple pass/fail scores, can significantly improve quantum education pedagogy.
main_problem: The paper addresses the lack of actionable pedagogical insights derived from detailed response logs generated by interactive quantum circuit simulators used in introductory quantum computing education.
main_result: A learning analytics framework was developed that successfully identifies bottleneck tasks, broad solution spaces, and recurring systematic errors not visible from final scores alone, enabling concrete course redesign.
method: The authors implemented a two-branch learning analytics pipeline analyzing submission logs across 21 circuit exercises, focusing on task-level diagnostics like first-attempt accuracy and answer-space profiling.
model_or_system: The system involves quantum circuits and quantum computing concepts, simulated via a drag-and-drop interface in the TIM learning environment. The analysis is performed on submission logs from an introductory course cohort.
key_observables: Task-level indicators include participation, completion rates, first-attempt accuracy, valid-attempt counts, and the observed answer-space (plain-text representation of submitted circuits).
important_parameters: The analysis covers 492 learners and 47,533 valid submissions across 21 obligatory exercises.
main_assumptions: The learner-level branch is an ongoing research extension, and the analysis is limited to the cohort data from one specific course run.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the two-branch pipeline, and ASCII visualizations (e.g., Fig. 2, Fig. 8) show the common correct and incorrect constructions observed in the answer space.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the two-branch learning analytics framework (task-level focus), presents the analysis of 21 exercises using process and outcome difficulty metrics, and concludes by demonstrating how these insights support actionable course redesign.
why_interesting: While the focus is educational, the rigorous analysis of systematic errors and solution space diversity in quantum circuit construction provides a model for analyzing complex, open-ended physical problem-solving in quantum contexts.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Two-branch learning analytics and EDM pipeline for TIM response logs. Both branches share the same source data and preprocessing, but differ in unit of analysis and resulting indicators. The task branch uses the 2024–2025 cohort (N=492) and provides the results reported in this paper. The learner-branch pilot uses the 2025–2026 cohort (N=209) and is included here only as a research-stage component of the broader framework.

Fig. 2. Compact example of the answer-space ASCII visualiser for tehtava-x-swap. The left column shows the two most common incorrect submitted constructions and the right column the two most common correct constructions, rendered as directly readable ASCII circuit schematics.

Fig. 3. Course progression by exercise in syllabus order. The solid line shows the number of learners who made at least one valid attempt on each exercise, and the dashed line shows the number who eventually solved it. Local drops indicate where the cohort thins out, and the separation between the curves shows outcome difficulty in count form: learners who reached an exercise but did not solve it. The figure therefore provides the first course-level view of bottlenecks before the more local exercise-level plots.

Figure 4 collates all four indicators across the 21 exercises. It is the exercise-level counterpart of the course-level gap in Fig. 3, but resolved by indicator: reading down a column locates the hardest exercises on that dimension, and reading across a row shows whether an exercise is broadly demanding or hard in one specific way.
